en: Udāna 4.1 Meghiyasutta Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Cālikā on Mount Cālikā.
Now at that time, the Venerable Meghiya was the Blessed One’s attendant.

Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and stood to one side. Standing to one side, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, I wish to enter Jantugāma for alms.
“Meghiya, do as you think it is now time to do.
Then, in the morning, the Venerable Meghiya dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Jantugāma for alms.
Having walked for alms in the village of Jantu and returned from his almsround after the meal, he approached the bank of the Kimikālā River.
As the Venerable Meghiya was walking and wandering back and forth along the bank of the Kimikālā River for exercise, he saw a mango grove that was inspiring, pleasing, and delightful.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to him:
“Truly, this mango grove is inspiring, delightful, and beautiful. It is indeed sufficient for a clansman seeking exertion to apply himself to spiritual striving.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would come to this mango grove to practice striving.
Then the Venerable Meghiya approached the Blessed One; having approached, he paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Jantu Village for alms.
Having walked for alms in Jantu Village and returned from my almsround after the meal, I approached the bank of the Kimikālā River.”
“Bhante, while walking and wandering for exercise along the bank of the Kimikālā River, I saw a mango grove that was inspiring, pleasing, and delightful.
Having seen it, this thought occurred to me:
‘Truly, this mango grove is inspiring, pleasing, and delightful.’”
“It would indeed be sufficient for a clansman seeking to strive for the sake of striving.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would come to this mango grove for the sake of striving.
“If the Blessed One grants me permission, venerable sir, I shall go to that mango grove for the sake of striving.”
When this was said, the Blessed One said to the Venerable Meghiya:
“Wait a moment, Meghiya; stay alone until some other monk arrives.
A second time, the Venerable Meghiya said to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for the Blessed One there is nothing further to be done, nor anything to be added to what has been done.
But for me, venerable sir, there is still more to be done, and there is yet to be added to what has been done.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would go to that mango grove to practice striving.”
A second time, the Blessed One said this to the Venerable Meghiya:
“Wait a moment, Meghiya; wait alone until some other monk arrives.
A third time, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, for the Blessed One there is nothing further to be done, nor anything to be added to what has been done.
But for me, venerable sir, there is something further to be done, and there is something to be added to what has been done.
If the Blessed One would grant me permission, I would go to that mango grove to practice striving.”
“Meghiya, when speaking of ‘striving,’ what could we possibly say?
Now, Meghiya, do as you think it is time.
Then the Venerable Meghiya rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him to his right, departed.
He approached that mango grove; having approached and entered deep into that mango grove, he sat down at the foot of a certain tree for his midday rest.
Then, as the Venerable Meghiya was dwelling in that mango grove, for the most part three kinds of evil, unwholesome thoughts occurred to him, namely:
“Sensual thought, thought of ill will, and thought of cruelty.
Then it occurred to the Venerable Meghiya:
“How wonderful, indeed! How marvelous, indeed!”
"Out of faith we have gone forth from the home life into homelessness;
yet we are still beset by these three evil, unwholesome thoughts, namely:
thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty."
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Meghiya emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One.
Having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the Venerable Meghiya said this to the Blessed One:
“Here, Bhante, while I was dwelling in that mango grove, for the most part three kinds of unwholesome, unskillful thoughts occurred to me:
namely, thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
Then, Bhante, it occurred to me:”
“It is wonderful indeed, sir! It is marvelous indeed, sir!
For we have gone forth from the home life into homelessness out of faith;
yet we are still beset by these three kinds of evil, unwholesome thoughts, namely:”
“By thoughts of sensual desire, thoughts of ill will, and thoughts of cruelty.
“Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, five things lead to its maturation.
What are the five?
"Here, Meghiya, a bhikkhu has good friends, good companions, and good associates.
For one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, Meghiya, this is the first quality that leads to its maturation.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training."
Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, this is the second thing that leads to its maturation.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu engages in discourse that is conducive to effacement, favorable to the opening of the mind, and leads to utter disenchantment, dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; that is to say, discourse on fewness of desires, and so forth.
Discourse on contentment, discourse on seclusion, discourse on non-association, discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration,
discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation;
he is one who gains such discourse at will, without difficulty, and without trouble.
Meghiya, for the maturation of the unripened liberation of mind, this is the third thing that leads to its maturation.

Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu dwells with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and the acquisition of wholesome states; he is steadfast, firm in his exertion, and does not lay down the burden regarding wholesome states.
Meghiya, for the maturation of the unripened liberation of mind, this is the fourth thing that leads to its maturation.
Furthermore, Meghiya, a bhikkhu is wise; he is endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away—noble, penetrative, and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
Meghiya, for one whose liberation of mind is not yet matured, this is the fifth quality that leads to its maturation.
Meghiya, these five qualities lead to the maturation of a liberation of mind that is not yet matured.
For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has a good companion, who has a good associate, it is to be expected that he will be virtuous,
that he will dwell restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults,
and that he will undertake and train himself in the rules of training.
For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has a good companion, who has a good associate,
it is to be expected that he will engage in whatever discourse is conducive to effacement, favorable to the opening of the mind, and leads to utter disenchantment,
dispassion, cessation, peace, direct knowledge, enlightenment, and Nibbāna; that is to say, a discourse on fewness of desires, a discourse on contentment, and so forth.
Discourse on seclusion, discourse on non-association, discourse on the arousal of energy, discourse on virtue, discourse on concentration,
discourse on wisdom, discourse on liberation, and discourse on the knowledge and vision of liberation— one will obtain such discourses at will, without difficulty, and without trouble.
For a bhikkhu who has a good friend, Meghiya, who has a good companion, who has a good associate, this is to be expected.
That he will dwell with energy aroused for the abandoning of unwholesome states and for the acquisition of wholesome states—
steadfast, firm in effort, not casting off the burden regarding wholesome states—
this, Meghiya, is to be expected of a bhikkhu who has a good friend, a good companion, and a good associate.
He will be wise, endowed with the wisdom that discerns arising and passing away— noble, penetrative,
and leading to the complete destruction of suffering.
And then, Meghiya, having established himself in these five qualities, that bhikkhu should further develop four qualities:

"The perception of foulness, Meghiya, should be developed for the abandoning of lust; loving-kindness should be developed for the abandoning of ill will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed for the cutting off of thought; and the perception of impermanence should be developed for the uprooting of the conceit 'I am.
For one who perceives impermanence, Meghiya, the perception of non-self becomes established;
one who perceives non-self reaches the uprooting of the conceit 'I am,' [and thus attains] Nibbāna in this very life."
Then the Blessed One, having understood this matter, on that occasion uttered this inspired exclamation:
“Trifling thoughts, subtle thoughts, Following along,
causing the mind to flutter;”
One who does not understand these thoughts of the mind runs from here to there with a wandering heart;
but one who understands these thoughts of the mind...
“Zealous and mindful, he restrains himself;
having abandoned without remainder those restless stirrings that follow after the mind, you are the Buddha.”
First.
